short: Money a company earns from activities outside its main business, such as interest on deposits, dividends or gains from selling investments.
kid: Your lemonade stand earns most of its coins by selling lemonade. One day your aunt gives you a coin for letting her park her bike in your yard. That coin is a bonus from something other than lemonade.
detail: Other income is a separate line in the profit and loss statement for earnings that do not come from a company's core operations. Typical items are interest on bank deposits and bonds, dividends from investments, rent from spare property, gains on selling assets or investments, and foreign exchange gains. In India, Schedule III of the Companies Act shows it just below revenue from operations. It matters because it can flatter profits: a company sitting on a large cash pile may report healthy profit even when its core business is weak. Analysts therefore strip it out when judging operating performance, and EBITDA is usually calculated without it. Watch for sudden jumps, which often come from one-time asset sales. For banks, interest is core revenue; their other income means fees, recoveries and treasury gains.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports revenue from operations of ₹500 crore and other income of ₹40 crore, of which ₹30 crore is interest on fixed deposits and ₹10 crore is a gain on selling an old warehouse. Total income is ₹540 crore. If profit before tax is ₹90 crore, ₹40 crore of it, about 44%, came from outside the core business.
formula: Total income = Revenue from operations + Other income

short: Unusual, large gains or losses, like a factory fire or a big asset sale, shown separately so a company's normal profit is easier to judge.
kid: Most weeks you get the same pocket money. One week your grandma gives you a big surprise gift. You keep that gift in a separate pile so you remember it will not happen every week.
detail: Exceptional items are income or expenses that are material and unusual in size or nature, so companies show them on a separate line to help readers see the underlying, repeatable profit. Examples include restructuring and redundancy costs, impairment write-downs, gains or losses on selling a business, legal settlements and losses from fires or floods. In India, the Schedule III format places exceptional items just above profit before tax. 'Extraordinary items' is an older, stricter label: IFRS and Ind AS forbid it and US GAAP dropped it in 2015, though it survives for companies on the older Indian accounting standards. The common trap is a company that reports 'one-off' charges every year; if they keep recurring, they are part of the business and analysts treat them as normal costs.
example: Say XYZ Ltd earns ₹120 crore of profit before exceptional items and tax, then books a ₹30 crore exceptional loss from a warehouse fire. Reported profit before tax falls to ₹90 crore, but an analyst judging the ongoing business would still start from ₹120 crore.
formula: Profit before tax = Profit before exceptional items and tax + Exceptional gains − Exceptional losses

short: A company's profit after all its costs, including interest and depreciation, but before income tax is deducted.
kid: You sell cookies and pay back everyone who helped you bake. Then you count the coins left over. This is that pile before you drop a few coins in the jar that pays for the town's parks and roads.
detail: Profit before tax is what remains after a company deducts every expense, including raw materials, salaries, depreciation, interest and any exceptional items, but before the income tax charge. It sits just above the tax line in the profit and loss statement. PBT is useful for comparing companies in different tax situations, say one enjoying a tax holiday or using past losses and another paying the full rate, because tax can make the final profit swing for reasons unrelated to the business. Do not confuse PBT with EBIT or operating profit: EBIT is before both interest and tax, so a heavily indebted company can show strong EBIT but weak PBT. Indian quarterly results often show profit both before and after exceptional items, so check which one a headline quotes.
example: Say ABC Ltd has revenue of ₹1,000 crore, operating costs of ₹750 crore, depreciation of ₹50 crore and interest of ₹40 crore. PBT is 1,000 − 750 − 50 − 40 = ₹160 crore. At a 25% tax rate, tax is ₹40 crore and net profit is ₹120 crore.
formula: PBT = Total income − All expenses except income tax

short: What a company has left from its revenue after paying every cost, including interest and income tax. It belongs to shareholders.
kid: You sell lemonade and pay for the lemons, the sugar and the cups, and drop a few coins in the jar for the town's parks. The coins still in your hand at the end are truly yours to keep.
detail: Net profit, also called profit after tax or net income, is the final line of the profit and loss statement: revenue and other income minus all expenses, including interest, depreciation, exceptional items and tax. It is the profit available to shareholders, either paid out as dividends or kept in the business as retained earnings, and it drives earnings per share and the P/E ratio. In consolidated accounts, net profit is split between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests, and only the parent's share is used for EPS. Two common mistakes: treating net profit as cash, when it includes non-cash items like depreciation and sales not yet collected, and ignoring one-offs that make a single quarter look much better or worse than the business really is.
example: Say ABC Ltd has profit before tax of ₹200 crore and a tax expense of ₹50 crore. Its net profit is ₹150 crore. With 10 crore shares outstanding, earnings per share are ₹15.
formula: Net profit = Profit before tax − Tax expense

short: Certain gains and losses, like swings in some investment values, foreign currency effects or pension estimates, reported below net profit instead of inside it.
kid: You have a box of trading cards you are not selling yet. Some weeks they seem worth more, some weeks less. You note those ups and downs on a separate page, away from your pocket-money page.
detail: Other comprehensive income is a section of the statement of profit and loss, placed below net profit, for gains and losses that accounting standards keep out of profit, usually because they are unrealised or long-term in nature. Under Ind AS and IFRS, typical items are value changes on equity investments the company has chosen to report through OCI, remeasurement of employee pension obligations, currency translation differences on overseas subsidiaries and gains or losses on cash flow hedges. Some items are later 'recycled' into profit when realised; others never are. Net profit plus OCI gives total comprehensive income, and OCI builds up in a reserve within equity. Large OCI losses cut book value even when net profit looks fine. A common confusion: OCI does not affect EPS, which uses net profit only.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports net profit of ₹80 crore. During the year, its long-term equity investments fall in value by ₹15 crore and translating its overseas subsidiary's accounts adds ₹5 crore (both after tax). OCI is −₹10 crore, so total comprehensive income is ₹70 crore, while EPS is still based on ₹80 crore.
formula: Total comprehensive income = Net profit + Other comprehensive income

short: Profit figures a company calculates its own way, outside official accounting rules, usually by removing items it calls one-off, like adjusted EBITDA.
kid: When you tell your friends your game score, you might say you would have had more if your brother had not bumped you. That is your own special score. The real score is still the one on the board.
detail: Non-GAAP measures are performance figures not defined by the accounting standards a company reports under, whether US GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles), IFRS or Ind AS. Common ones are EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, adjusted net profit, adjusted EPS and free cash flow. Management builds them by removing items it calls non-recurring or non-cash, such as stock-based compensation, restructuring costs or impairments. Used honestly, they reveal underlying trends. The danger is that each company picks its own adjustments, so figures are not comparable across firms and can be inflated by excluding real, recurring costs. Regulators therefore demand a reconciliation to the nearest official figure: the SEC in the US and ESMA guidelines in Europe, while IFRS 18, effective from 2027, brings management-defined measures into audited notes. Always read the reconciliation before trusting the headline.
example: Say ABC Inc reports net income of $50 million. It adds back $20 million of stock-based compensation and $10 million of 'one-time' restructuring costs to show adjusted net income of $80 million. If restructuring charges appear every year, the $80 million overstates what the business really earns.
formula: Adjusted profit = Reported profit + Items management chooses to exclude

short: A cost recorded in the profit and loss statement that does not involve paying out cash in that period, like depreciation or a write-down.
kid: You paid for your bike long ago. This year you pay nothing, but the bike still gets a bit more scratched and worn. Noting that wear, without spending a coin, is what this is.
detail: A non-cash expense reduces reported profit without any cash leaving the business in that period. The biggest examples are depreciation and amortisation, which spread the cost of assets bought earlier over their useful lives. Others include impairment write-downs, stock-based compensation, allowances for bad debts and unrealised losses on investments. Because profit falls but cash does not, the indirect-method cash flow statement adds these items back to net profit to arrive at cash from operations. This is why a company can report a loss yet generate cash, and why EBITDA, which excludes depreciation and amortisation, is popular. The confusion to avoid: non-cash does not mean free. Depreciation reflects real money spent on assets in the past, and stock-based compensation dilutes shareholders, so ignoring these costs overstates true earnings.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports net profit of ₹30 crore after charging ₹25 crore of depreciation and a ₹5 crore impairment. Ignoring working capital changes, its cash from operations is about 30 + 25 + 5 = ₹60 crore, double the reported profit.
formula: Cash from operations (indirect method) = Net profit + Non-cash expenses ± Changes in working capital

short: The accounting method of spreading the cost of a long-lasting asset, like a machine or building, over the years it is used.
kid: You buy a scooter that will last you five years. Instead of saying it cost everything on the first day, you count a little piece of its price for each year you ride it.
detail: Depreciation allocates the cost of tangible fixed assets, such as machinery, vehicles, computers and buildings, over their useful life, because these assets help earn revenue for many years. Each year's share is an expense in the profit and loss statement, and the running total is deducted from the asset's cost on the balance sheet as accumulated depreciation. The two main methods are straight-line, which charges an equal amount each year, and written-down value, which charges more in early years. In India, Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013 sets indicative useful lives, while the Income Tax Act uses its own block-wise rates, so book and tax depreciation usually differ. Land is not depreciated. Depreciation is a non-cash expense and is not a measure of falling market value. In rupee news, 'depreciation' means a currency weakening, a different idea.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys a machine for ₹10 lakh, expects to use it for 8 years and then sell it as scrap for ₹2 lakh. Straight-line depreciation is (10 − 2) / 8 = ₹1 lakh a year, so after 3 years the machine sits on the books at ₹7 lakh.
formula: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost − Salvage value) / Useful life

short: Spreading the cost of an intangible asset, such as software, a licence or a patent, as an expense over the years it is useful.
kid: You buy a pool pass that works for a whole year. You cannot hold the swimming in your hand, but you can count a little bit of the pass's price for every month you use it.
detail: Amortisation is the intangible-asset version of depreciation. It spreads the cost of assets you cannot touch, such as software, patents, licences, brands bought in an acquisition, telecom spectrum or toll-road rights, over the period they are expected to bring benefits, usually in equal yearly amounts. Under Ind AS and IFRS, goodwill and intangibles with indefinite lives are not amortised; they are tested for impairment every year instead. Like depreciation, amortisation is a non-cash expense, which is why EBITDA adds it back. For Indian telecom and infrastructure companies, amortisation of spectrum and concession rights can be large enough to turn a strong operating profit into a loss. The word has a second meaning in lending: amortising a loan means repaying principal gradually through instalments, as in an EMI schedule.
example: Say ABC Ltd pays ₹50 crore for a 10-year licence to make a patented drug. It records amortisation of 50 / 10 = ₹5 crore a year, so after 4 years the licence is carried at ₹30 crore.
formula: Annual amortisation = (Cost − Residual value) / Useful life

short: The total depreciation charged on an asset since it was bought, subtracted from its original cost to show its current book value.
kid: Every year you put a small sticker on your bike to show it got a bit more used. Counting all the stickers tells you how much of the bike you have used up so far.
detail: Accumulated depreciation is the running total of all depreciation recorded on an asset, or group of assets, since it was put to use. Instead of reducing the asset's cost directly, accountants keep the original cost (the gross block) and record accumulated depreciation alongside it, so the balance sheet shows both what was paid and how much has been used up. Cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment gives the net carrying amount, or net block. When an asset is sold or scrapped, both its cost and its accumulated depreciation are removed. Analysts find it useful: a high ratio of accumulated depreciation to gross block suggests an ageing asset base that may soon need heavy capex. Despite the older Indian label 'provision for depreciation', it is a deduction from assets, not a pile of cash saved for replacement.
example: Say ABC Ltd bought machinery for ₹40 lakh and charges ₹5 lakh of depreciation a year. After 6 years, accumulated depreciation is ₹30 lakh and the net book value is 40 − 30 = ₹10 lakh.
formula: Net book value = Cost − Accumulated depreciation − Accumulated impairment

short: A depreciation method that charges the same amount every year, by spreading cost minus scrap value evenly over the asset's life.
kid: You have twelve cookies to last twelve days. You eat exactly one every day, the same each day, until they are all gone.
detail: Under the straight-line method, an asset's depreciable amount, its cost minus expected salvage value, is divided equally across each year of its useful life, so the expense is the same every year. It is the simplest and most widely used method in company accounts worldwide, and many large Indian companies use it in their books under Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013. It suits assets that wear out evenly, such as buildings, furniture or long-lived plant. Compared with the written-down value method, it gives lower depreciation and higher profit in the early years, and the reverse later. A common confusion: the percentage rate (say 10% a year for a 10-year life) applies to the original depreciable amount every year, not to the shrinking book value.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys a delivery van for ₹12 lakh with a useful life of 5 years and a salvage value of ₹2 lakh. Annual depreciation is (12 − 2) / 5 = ₹2 lakh, so the book value falls from ₹12 lakh to ₹10, ₹8, ₹6, ₹4 and finally ₹2 lakh.
formula: Annual depreciation = (Cost − Salvage value) / Useful life

short: A depreciation method that charges a fixed percentage on the asset's remaining book value each year, so charges are biggest early and shrink later.
kid: You have a big bowl of popcorn, and each day you eat half of what is left. On the first day you eat a lot, and every day after you eat a little less.
detail: Under the written-down value method, each year's depreciation is a fixed rate applied to the asset's opening book value, which is cost minus all depreciation charged so far. Because the base shrinks, the charge is highest in the first year and falls every year after, which suits assets like computers and vehicles that lose usefulness quickly. The rate needed to reach a chosen salvage value is 1 − (Salvage value / Cost)^(1 / Useful life). In India, the Income Tax Act uses block-wise WDV depreciation, and many companies also use WDV in their books, so it is far more common here than in markets where company accounts mostly use straight-line. A common error is applying the rate to original cost every year, which is really the straight-line method. Under WDV, book value never quite reaches zero.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys a machine for ₹10 lakh and depreciates it at 20% WDV. Year 1 depreciation is ₹2 lakh (book value ₹8 lakh), year 2 is ₹1.6 lakh (book value ₹6.4 lakh) and year 3 is ₹1.28 lakh (book value ₹5.12 lakh).
formula: Depreciation = Opening book value × Rate; Rate = 1 − (Salvage value / Cost)^(1 / Useful life)

short: The amount a company expects to get for an asset when it stops using it, such as by selling it second-hand or as scrap.
kid: When your old bicycle gets too small for you, you can still sell it to a younger child for a few coins. Those few coins are what this means.
detail: Salvage value is the estimated amount a company expects to recover from an asset at the end of its useful life, after deducting the costs of disposal. It is subtracted from cost before calculating depreciation, because only the part of the asset that will actually be used up should be charged as an expense. Under Ind AS 16 and IAS 16, residual value and useful life must be reviewed at least at each financial year end, with changes applied going forward. Schedule II of the Indian Companies Act treats 5% of original cost as the normal ceiling for residual value, with higher figures allowed if justified and disclosed, under the rules as of 2025. Setting salvage value too high lowers depreciation and flatters profit. Do not confuse it with today's market value, or with terminal value in a DCF valuation.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys a truck for ₹30 lakh, expects to use it for 6 years and then sell it as scrap for ₹1.5 lakh, which is 5% of cost. Only ₹28.5 lakh is depreciated, giving straight-line depreciation of ₹4.75 lakh a year.
formula: Depreciable amount = Cost − Salvage value

short: The number of years, or units of output, over which a company expects an asset to be useful to its business.
kid: Your school bag will probably last about three years before it gets too worn out. Those three years are how long it is useful to you.
detail: Useful life is management's estimate of how long an asset will be used by the business, expressed in years or in output such as machine hours or kilometres. It drives depreciation and amortisation: the longer the useful life, the smaller the yearly charge and the higher the reported profit. It can be shorter than the asset's physical life, for instance when a company replaces laptops every three years even though they could run for six. In India, under the rules as of 2025, Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013 gives indicative lives, such as 30 years for factory buildings and 3 years for end-user computers; companies may use different estimates if they justify them. Ind AS 16 requires a review at least every year end. Watch for companies that stretch useful lives to cut depreciation, a quiet way to boost earnings.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys servers for ₹6 crore with no salvage value. Over a 6-year useful life, depreciation is ₹1 crore a year; if management stretched the estimate to 8 years, it would drop to ₹75 lakh, lifting profit before tax by ₹25 lakh a year.

short: Things a company owns that will turn into cash or be used up within a year, like cash, unsold goods and customer dues.
kid: At your lemonade stand, the coins in your box, the lemons in your basket and the coins your friend promised to pay tomorrow will all be used or turned into coins very soon.
detail: Current assets are assets a company expects to turn into cash, sell or use up within twelve months or within its normal operating cycle. The main ones are cash and cash equivalents, short-term investments, trade receivables, inventories, short-term loans and advances, and prepaid expenses. Under Schedule III in India, the operating cycle is assumed to be twelve months when it cannot be clearly identified. Current assets fund day-to-day operations and, compared with current liabilities, show whether a company can pay its near-term bills, through the current ratio and working capital. A common confusion is treating all current assets as equally liquid: cash is usable immediately, but slow-moving inventory or dues from struggling customers may take months to convert, or may never be collected.
example: Say ABC Ltd has cash of ₹20 crore, receivables of ₹35 crore, inventory of ₹40 crore and prepaid expenses of ₹5 crore. Its current assets total ₹100 crore. If current liabilities are ₹80 crore, the current ratio is 100 / 80 = 1.25.
formula: Current assets = Cash and cash equivalents + Short-term investments + Receivables + Inventory + Other current assets

short: Things a company owns and expects to keep or use for more than a year, like factories, machines, patents and long-term investments.
kid: Your lemonade stand has a table and a big jug you will use summer after summer. You are not going to sell them soon; they help you make lemonade for a long time.
detail: Non-current assets are resources a company expects to benefit from for more than twelve months or beyond its operating cycle. They include property, plant and equipment, capital work in progress, intangible assets and goodwill, long-term investments, long-term loans and deposits, and deferred tax assets. They are the base that produces revenue over many years and are usually funded by long-term sources such as equity and long-term borrowings. Their share of total assets shows how capital-intensive a business is: a steel maker is dominated by non-current assets, while a software services firm has comparatively few. A common confusion is to think non-current means impossible to sell; listed shares held as long-term investments can be sold within days, they are simply not meant to be.
example: Say ABC Ltd has net PP&E of ₹300 crore, capital work in progress of ₹50 crore, intangibles of ₹30 crore and long-term investments of ₹20 crore. Its non-current assets are ₹400 crore. If total assets are ₹500 crore, 80% of its asset base is long term.
formula: Non-current assets = Total assets − Current assets

short: Amounts a company owes that must be paid within about a year, such as bills to suppliers, short-term loans and unpaid wages.
kid: You borrowed two coins from your friend and promised to give them back on Friday. Things you must pay back very soon, like those two coins, are what this means.
detail: Current liabilities are obligations a company expects to settle within twelve months or its normal operating cycle. They include trade payables, short-term borrowings, the part of long-term loans due within the year (current maturities), accrued expenses, interest payable, advances received from customers, tax payable and short-term provisions. Compared with current assets, they show near-term liquidity through the current ratio and working capital. Rising current liabilities are not always bad: a retailer or FMCG company that gets long credit from suppliers is effectively using supplier money to run its business. The real warning signs are short-term borrowings piling up, or long-term debt falling due without enough cash to repay it. A common miss is overlooking current maturities of long-term debt, which can be large.
example: Say ABC Ltd owes suppliers ₹45 crore, has a ₹20 crore working capital loan, ₹10 crore of long-term debt due this year and ₹5 crore of accrued salaries. Its current liabilities total ₹80 crore.
formula: Current liabilities = Trade payables + Short-term borrowings + Current maturities of long-term debt + Accrued expenses + Other current liabilities

short: Amounts a company owes that are not due for more than a year, such as long-term loans, bonds and lease obligations.
kid: You borrowed coins from Grandpa to buy a big bike, and he said you can pay him back slowly over many birthdays. That is a promise for a long time away.
detail: Non-current liabilities are obligations not due for settlement within twelve months or the operating cycle. They include long-term borrowings such as term loans, debentures and bonds, long-term lease liabilities, deferred tax liabilities, and long-term provisions such as gratuity and pension obligations. Together with equity, they fund long-lived assets like plants and infrastructure. Analysts use them in leverage measures such as debt-to-equity and in judging solvency, a company's ability to survive over the long run. Each year, the portion of long-term debt due in the next twelve months moves to current liabilities, so a fall in non-current debt may simply mean repayment is approaching, not that debt has been cleared. Also note that some items here, like deferred tax liabilities, are not borrowings at all.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a ₹200 crore term loan repayable in equal yearly instalments of ₹40 crore over five years. Today ₹40 crore is shown under current liabilities and ₹160 crore under non-current liabilities.
formula: Non-current liabilities = Total liabilities − Current liabilities

short: Money in hand or in the bank, plus very safe investments that turn into a known amount of cash within about three months.
kid: The coins in your pocket and in your piggy bank are money you can spend right away. This is all the money you can grab quickly whenever you need it.
detail: Cash and cash equivalents is the most liquid line on the balance sheet. Cash means currency and bank deposits that can be withdrawn on demand. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that convert readily into a known amount of cash with very little risk of a change in value, typically with an original maturity of three months or less, such as treasury bills, commercial paper and short bank deposits. The cash flow statement explains how this balance moved from the start to the end of the period. Investors watch it to judge whether a company can pay its bills, survive a downturn or fund growth without borrowing. A common confusion: in India, longer fixed deposits sit under 'other bank balances' and liquid mutual fund holdings under current investments, so total liquidity can be much larger. Net cash also deducts debt.
example: Say ABC Ltd holds ₹5 crore in current accounts, ₹15 crore in bank deposits maturing within three months and ₹30 crore in a one-year fixed deposit. Cash and cash equivalents are ₹20 crore; the one-year deposit is reported separately, even though the company's total liquid funds are ₹50 crore.

short: Money customers owe a company for goods or services it has already delivered but not yet been paid for.
kid: You gave your friend a cup of lemonade, and she said she will pay you tomorrow. Until she pays, those coins are owed to you.
detail: Accounts receivable, shown as trade receivables in Indian balance sheets, are amounts customers owe for sales made on credit. When a company sells on credit, it records the revenue immediately along with a receivable, and turns it into cash when the customer pays. Receivables are a current asset and a big part of working capital. Analysts track receivable days, or debtor days: how many days of sales are waiting to be collected. Receivables growing much faster than revenue can signal lenient credit terms, weak customers or even inflated sales, and they tie up cash. Under Ind AS, companies must set aside an allowance for amounts unlikely to be collected, using the expected credit loss model. In India, dues from government departments and state power distributors are notoriously slow, which is why small suppliers sell their bills early on the RBI-regulated TReDS platforms.
example: Say ABC Ltd has annual revenue of ₹365 crore and trade receivables of ₹60 crore. Daily sales are ₹1 crore, so receivable days are 60 / 1 = 60, meaning customers take about two months to pay.
formula: Receivable days = Trade receivables / Revenue × 365

short: Money owed by customers that a company does not expect to collect, written off or set aside as a loss.
kid: You gave your friend three cookies and he promised to pay you later, but then he moved away. You will probably never get paid, so you stop counting those coins as yours.
detail: Bad debts are receivables a company concludes it will not collect, for example because a customer has gone bankrupt. A confirmed bad debt is written off, reducing receivables and booking an expense. Before that point, companies keep an allowance, once called a provision for doubtful debts, for amounts likely to go unpaid. Under Ind AS 109 and IFRS 9, this follows the expected credit loss (ECL) model: companies provide for losses they expect, using past experience and forward-looking information, rather than waiting for a default. Trade receivables usually use a simple provision matrix based on how overdue each bill is. Banks apply the same idea to loans; under the RBI's plans as of 2025, Indian banks are due to move from incurred-loss provisioning to ECL from April 2027. Analysts watch for allowances that look too small against ageing receivables, which flatters profit.
example: Say ABC Ltd has trade receivables of ₹100 crore: ₹80 crore not yet due, ₹15 crore overdue by up to 90 days and ₹5 crore overdue by more than a year. Using loss rates of 1%, 10% and 60%, its ECL allowance is 0.8 + 1.5 + 3 = ₹5.3 crore, and net receivables are ₹94.7 crore.
formula: Net receivables = Gross trade receivables − Allowance for expected credit losses

short: Goods a company holds to sell, plus the raw materials and half-finished products it will turn into goods for sale.
kid: Your lemonade stand keeps lemons, sugar and a few bottles already made, waiting for customers. Everything on your shelf waiting to be sold or used is this.
detail: Inventory is a current asset made up of raw materials, work in progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade bought for resale, and stores and spares. Under Ind AS 2 and IAS 2, it is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, so goods that can only be sold below cost must be written down. Cost is assigned using FIFO or weighted average; LIFO is not allowed. When goods are sold, their cost moves from the balance sheet to cost of goods sold. Analysts track inventory days or turnover: piling inventory can mean weak demand or obsolete goods, or a deliberate build-up before a busy season like Diwali. 'Channel inventory' in news means goods sitting with dealers, not the company. In Indian accounts, 'stock' often means inventory, not shares.
example: Say ABC Ltd has average inventory of ₹60 crore and cost of goods sold of ₹300 crore a year. Inventory turnover is 300 / 60 = 5 times, so goods sit for about 365 / 5 = 73 days before being sold.
formula: Inventory days = Average inventory / Cost of goods sold × 365

short: An inventory method that assumes the oldest goods are sold first, so the cost of what is sold is based on older purchase prices.
kid: When you line up for the slide, the child who came first goes down first. With a jar of sweets, you eat the ones you put in first before the newer ones.
detail: FIFO is a cost-flow assumption for valuing inventory: goods bought or made first are treated as sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects older costs and closing inventory reflects the most recent prices. It need not match how goods physically move, though for perishables it usually does. When prices are rising, FIFO gives a lower cost of goods sold, higher profit and a balance-sheet inventory close to current prices, but also higher taxable profit. Under Ind AS 2 and IFRS, companies may use FIFO or weighted average cost, while LIFO is banned, so FIFO is common among Indian manufacturers and retailers. A common confusion: FIFO does not change the total cost of inventory over time, only how it is split between periods, and between the profit and loss statement and the balance sheet.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys 100 units at ₹10 and later 100 units at ₹12, then sells 150 units. Under FIFO, cost of goods sold is 100 × 10 + 50 × 12 = ₹1,600, and the 50 units left are valued at 50 × 12 = ₹600.

short: An inventory method that assumes the newest goods are sold first; allowed in the US but banned under Indian and international accounting standards.
kid: Imagine a stack of plates. You put new plates on top and always take the top one first, so the newest plate gets used before the old ones at the bottom.
detail: LIFO assumes the most recently bought or made goods are sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects the latest costs while closing inventory carries older, often much lower, costs. When prices rise, LIFO increases cost of goods sold, lowers reported profit and reduces income tax, which is why some US companies use it; US tax rules allow it only if it is also used in the financial statements. IFRS and Ind AS prohibit LIFO because balance-sheet inventory can become badly outdated. US companies on LIFO disclose a LIFO reserve, the gap between FIFO and LIFO inventory values, which analysts add back to compare them with FIFO peers. A trap to watch: if a LIFO company sells down old layers of inventory, very old, low costs flow into profit and inflate it temporarily.
example: Say ABC Inc buys 100 units at $10 and later 100 units at $12, then sells 150 units. Under LIFO, cost of goods sold is 100 × 12 + 50 × 10 = $1,700, which is $100 more than under FIFO, and the 50 units left are valued at $500.
formula: FIFO inventory = LIFO inventory + LIFO reserve

short: Payments a company makes in advance for goods or services it will receive later, such as a year's rent or insurance paid upfront.
kid: You pay the ice-cream man today for an ice cream he will bring you every Saturday this month. You have paid, but you have not eaten them yet, so they are still waiting for you.
detail: Prepaid expenses arise when a company pays before it receives the related benefit, such as insurance premiums, rent, software subscriptions or maintenance contracts paid in advance. Under accrual accounting, the payment is first recorded as a current asset, because the company is owed a future service, and is then moved to the profit and loss statement as an expense over the period the service is used. This matches the cost to the period that benefits from it. Prepaid expenses are usually small, but sudden jumps can hint at costs being parked on the balance sheet to flatter current profit. Do not confuse them with accrued expenses, the mirror image: services already received but not yet paid for. And 'prepayment' of a loan is a different idea altogether: repaying it early.
example: Say ABC Ltd pays ₹12 lakh on 1 January for a full year of factory insurance. By the end of March, ₹3 lakh has been used up and charged as an expense, while ₹9 lakh remains on the balance sheet as a prepaid expense.

short: Costs a company has already run up, such as staff wages or electricity used, but has not yet paid by the reporting date.
kid: A neighbour looked after you on Friday and will be paid next week. The work is done, but the coins have not been handed over yet, so they are still owed.
detail: Accrued expenses are liabilities for costs a company has incurred but not yet paid, or even been billed for, at the balance-sheet date: salaries for the last days of the month, interest building up on a loan, electricity, professional fees and bonuses. Accrual accounting records an expense in the period it relates to, not when the cash goes out, so the company books the expense and a matching current liability; payment later clears the liability. Indian books traditionally call them outstanding expenses. They differ from trade payables, which are backed by a supplier's invoice, and from provisions, which involve more uncertainty about amount or timing. Analysts watch them as part of working capital: rising accruals boost operating cash flow temporarily, because the cash is paid later.
example: Say ABC Ltd took a ₹1 crore loan at 12% a year on 1 January, with interest paid each 31 December. At 31 March, three months of interest, ₹1 crore × 12% × 3/12 = ₹3 lakh, is booked as an expense and as an accrued liability.

short: Money a company owes its suppliers for goods or services it has received but not yet paid for.
kid: The shopkeeper gave you lemons for your stand and said you can pay him at the end of the week. Until you pay, you owe him those coins.
detail: Accounts payable, shown as trade payables in Indian balance sheets, are amounts a company owes suppliers for goods and services bought on credit. They are a current liability and a key part of working capital. Analysts track payable days: how long, on average, the company takes to pay its suppliers. Longer supplier credit frees up cash, and strong businesses such as large FMCG firms and retailers use it as interest-free funding. But stretching suppliers too far can damage relationships or signal cash stress. In India, Schedule III requires separate disclosure of dues to micro and small enterprises. Under the tax rules as of 2025 (section 43B(h) of the Income Tax Act, 1961), such dues paid after the legal deadline of 15 days, or up to 45 by agreement, are deductible only in the year actually paid. Do not confuse trade payables with borrowings, although supplier-finance schemes can blur the line.
example: Say ABC Ltd has trade payables of ₹40 crore and buys ₹292 crore a year from suppliers. Payable days are 40 / 292 × 365 = 50, so it pays suppliers about 50 days after buying.
formula: Payable days = Trade payables / Purchases (or cost of goods sold) × 365

short: The money tied up in a company's day-to-day operations: current assets like unsold goods and customer dues, minus current liabilities like supplier bills.
kid: To run your lemonade stand each day, you need lemons, cups and some coins for change. Take away what you still owe the shopkeeper, and what is left is what you need just to keep going.
detail: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It measures the short-term funds a business needs for daily operations: buying raw materials, holding inventory and waiting for customers to pay, offset by credit received from suppliers. Analysts often use operating working capital, which leaves out cash and short-term borrowings, to focus on the business itself. Positive working capital means short-term assets cover short-term obligations, but too much means cash is stuck in inventory and receivables. Negative working capital is not always a red flag: supermarkets, FMCG makers and online platforms often collect from customers before paying suppliers, so growth generates cash rather than consuming it. An increase in working capital is a use of cash in the cash flow statement, which is why fast-growing firms can be profitable yet short of cash.
example: Say ABC Ltd has inventory of ₹50 crore, receivables of ₹40 crore and cash of ₹10 crore, against trade payables of ₹45 crore and other current liabilities of ₹15 crore. Working capital is (50 + 40 + 10) − (45 + 15) = ₹40 crore.
formula: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

short: Physical assets a company uses for years to run its business, such as land, buildings, machinery, vehicles and computers.
kid: Your lemonade stand has a table, a big jug and a sign you painted. You use them every day, summer after summer, to make and sell lemonade.
detail: Property, plant and equipment are physical assets held for producing goods or services, for renting out or for administration, and expected to be used for more than a year. They include land, buildings, plant and machinery, furniture, vehicles and office equipment. Under Ind AS 16 and IAS 16, PP&E is recorded at cost, including purchase price, duties, installation and borrowing costs during construction, and then depreciated over its useful life; land is not depreciated. Companies may instead revalue a whole class of assets to fair value. Indian balance sheets show the gross block, accumulated depreciation and the resulting net block, with assets still being built shown separately as capital work in progress. PP&E-heavy sectors such as steel, cement and power need large, ongoing capex. Goods held for sale are inventory, not PP&E.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys a machine for ₹80 lakh, pays ₹5 lakh in freight and ₹15 lakh to install it. The machine is recorded in PP&E at ₹1 crore, not ₹80 lakh, and depreciation is calculated on the full ₹1 crore.
formula: Net PP&E = Gross PP&E − Accumulated depreciation − Accumulated impairment

short: The total original cost of a company's fixed assets, such as land, buildings and machinery, before subtracting any depreciation.
kid: Add up the price of every toy you have ever bought and still own, even the old, scratched ones. That big total, as if they were all still new, is what this means.
detail: Gross block is an Indian accounting term for the total cost at which a company's property, plant and equipment, and often its intangible assets, are carried before deducting accumulated depreciation and impairment. It rises with additions from capex or acquisitions and falls when assets are sold or scrapped. Analysts use it to measure investment in productive capacity and asset intensity, for example through the fixed asset turnover ratio. Comparing gross block with net block shows how old the assets are: if most of the gross block has been depreciated, heavy replacement spending may be near. Gross block usually excludes capital work in progress, which joins it only when the asset is ready for use. The term is mainly Indian; elsewhere you will see gross PP&E.
example: Say ABC Ltd starts the year with a gross block of ₹500 crore, adds ₹80 crore of new machinery and scraps old equipment that originally cost ₹30 crore. Its closing gross block is 500 + 80 − 30 = ₹550 crore.
formula: Closing gross block = Opening gross block + Additions − Disposals

short: The value of a company's fixed assets on its books: their original cost minus all depreciation and write-downs charged so far.
kid: Your bike cost a lot when it was new, but now it is a few years old and a bit worn. What it counts for now, after all that wear, is this.
detail: Net block is the carrying value of a company's fixed assets: gross block minus accumulated depreciation and impairment. It is the figure that actually counts in total assets on the balance sheet, and a key input for return ratios such as return on capital employed. It shrinks every year through depreciation and grows when the company spends on new assets. A net block falling while gross block stays flat suggests an ageing asset base, while a sharp jump usually follows a big capex cycle or acquisition. Analysts sometimes add capital work in progress to see total investment, but strictly it is shown separately. A common confusion: net block is a book value based on historical cost, not what the assets would fetch if sold today; land bought decades ago may be worth many times its book value.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a gross block of ₹550 crore and accumulated depreciation of ₹220 crore. Its net block is ₹330 crore, meaning 40% of the original cost has already been depreciated.
formula: Net block = Gross block − Accumulated depreciation − Accumulated impairment

short: Money spent on assets still being built or installed, such as a factory under construction, which are not yet ready for use.
kid: You are building a big treehouse and have bought the wood and nails, but it is only half done. You cannot play in it yet, but you have already spent your coins on it.
detail: Capital work in progress is a non-current asset that collects the cost of property, plant and equipment not yet ready for its intended use: plants under construction, machinery awaiting installation, and related costs such as borrowing costs and directly attributable pre-operative expenses. CWIP is not depreciated. Once the asset is ready for use, its cost moves to the gross block and depreciation begins. For capital-heavy Indian sectors such as power, cement, steel and infrastructure, CWIP shows how much future capacity is in the pipeline. Schedule III requires an ageing schedule showing how long projects have sat in CWIP and whether they are overdue or over budget. A large CWIP balance that keeps growing without being capitalised can signal delays, cost overruns or costs being parked to avoid depreciation.
example: Say ABC Ltd has spent ₹300 crore so far on a cement plant, including ₹20 crore of capitalised interest. The full ₹300 crore sits in CWIP with no depreciation; once production starts, it moves to the gross block, and with a 25-year life and no salvage value, straight-line depreciation would be ₹12 crore a year.

short: Money a company spends to buy, build or upgrade long-lasting assets, such as factories, machines or technology, that will serve it for years.
kid: Buying lemons is for today's lemonade. Buying a bigger, stronger table for your stand is for many summers to come, and that bigger kind of spending is what this means.
detail: Capital expenditure is spending on assets that will benefit the business for more than a year: plants, machinery, buildings, technology, mines or networks, plus major upgrades that extend an asset's life. Unlike operating expenses such as salaries or rent, capex is not charged to the profit and loss statement at once; it is added to PP&E, or to CWIP while under construction, and expensed gradually through depreciation. In the cash flow statement it is an outflow under investing activities, and free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capex. Analysts split it into maintenance capex, needed to keep existing capacity running, and growth capex, which adds capacity. Indian 'capex cycle' headlines track whether companies and the government, whose budget calls it capital outlay, are investing heavily. Capex is not a cost that vanishes; it builds assets.
example: Say ABC Ltd generates ₹400 crore of operating cash flow and spends ₹250 crore on a new production line and ₹50 crore replacing old machines. Total capex is ₹300 crore and free cash flow is 400 − 300 = ₹100 crore.
formula: Capex ≈ Closing net PP&E (including CWIP) − Opening net PP&E (including CWIP) + Depreciation for the year

short: Recording a cost as an asset on the balance sheet, to be expensed over future years, instead of as an expense right away.
kid: When you spend coins on sweets, they are gone today. When you spend coins on a sturdy box to keep your toys in for years, you remember it as something you still have.
detail: Capitalisation means adding a cost to the value of an asset instead of charging it to the profit and loss statement immediately. It applies when spending creates a future benefit: a machine's price plus freight, installation and testing; interest on loans used to build a qualifying asset, under Ind AS 23 and IAS 23; and development costs for software or products once strict conditions such as technical feasibility are met. The capitalised amount is later depreciated or amortised. Capitalising raises current profit, pushes costs into future years and shows the cash under investing rather than operating activities, flattering operating cash flow. That makes it a classic area for manipulation: WorldCom's fraud involved booking billions of dollars of ordinary line costs as capex. This is unrelated to market capitalisation, a company's stock market value.
example: Say ABC Ltd spends ₹10 crore developing new software it expects to use for 5 years. If it expenses the cost, this year's profit falls by ₹10 crore. If it capitalises it, profit falls by only ₹2 crore of amortisation a year for 5 years.

short: Valuable assets with no physical form, such as patents, brands, software, licences and customer relationships, that help a company earn money.
kid: Your secret lemonade recipe and the name everyone on your street knows, Sunny Lemonade, cannot be touched like a jug. But they still make people come to your stand.
detail: Intangible assets are identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights, software, licences, telecom spectrum and customer contracts acquired in a deal. Under Ind AS 38 and IAS 38, they are recognised only if the company controls them, they will bring future economic benefits and their cost can be measured reliably. Purchased intangibles are recorded at cost, but most home-grown ones, such as a brand built through years of advertising, are not recognised at all, and research costs are always expensed. Intangibles with finite lives are amortised, while those with indefinite lives, and goodwill, are tested for impairment instead. This is why brand-led consumer and technology companies often look far more valuable in the market than on paper. Goodwill is usually shown separately from other intangibles.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys a rival's brand for ₹200 crore and expects to benefit from it for 20 years. It records a ₹200 crore intangible asset and amortises it by ₹10 crore a year, while its own brand, built over decades, does not appear on the balance sheet at all.
